html:
A period in the first half of the 1700s when drinking of cheap gin soared in Britain, above all among the poor of London.

Gin came from the Dutch drink jenever. After William III came to the throne, the government taxed French brandy heavily and freed anyone to distil spirits from English grain, which helped landowners sell their crops. Gin became very cheap, and was sold from thousands of small shops, stalls and barrows.

Critics blamed it for crime, neglect of children and early death. In 1751 William Hogarth printed Gin Lane, a street of ruin, next to Beer Street, where healthy people drink beer. Laws tried to curb the trade, and the Gin Act of 1736 failed, but the Gin Act of 1751, with higher fees and better policing, along with dearer grain, ended the craze.

The historian Fernand Braudel sets the craze in a wider story. From the 1500s, distilled spirits spread through Europe, and for people living on poor diets strong drink was a cheap comfort and a source of calories.
sum: A period in the first half of the 1700s when drinking of cheap gin soared in Britain, above all among the poor of London.
